title: EIP-8173: Foundations of EVM Control Flow
description: Understanding EVM control flow and its relation to Ethereum's scaling roadmap
author: Greg Colvin (@gcolvin)
bodyPreview: ## Abstract The Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM) provides no instructions for calls and returns within a contract, and no validation of deployed code: compilers synthesize calls with dynamic jumps. In this the EVM is an anomaly — the JVM, the CLR, Wasm, and nearly every blockchain VM require validated static control flow, supported by native calls and returns. Static control flow is traversed in linear time. Dynamic jumps create dynamic control flow, which makes traversal quadratic and walking the paths factorial — twenty-nine bytes of code can cost nearly a million walks. Dynamic control flow is a denial-of-service risk for online validation and compilation, a burden on formal analysis, and an obstacle to zero-knowledge (ZK) proving and RISC-V on the scaling roadmap. This document lays out the history and the costs. It serves as background for past and current proposals for static control flow — and for discussions still to come. _Note: Significant assistance from AI is acknowledged, primarily for research, the figures, and the demonstration programs._ ## Motivation ### Historical Context #### Babbage 1833: Jumps and Conditional Jumps In 1833 Charles Babbage began the design of the Analytical Engine: a steam-powered, mechanical, Turing-complete computer. Programs were to be encoded on punched cards that controlled a system of rods, gears, and other machinery to implement arithmetic, storage (for 1,000 40-digit decimal numbers), and conditional jumps. Jumps were supported by cards that shuffled the card deck forwards or backwards a fixed number of cards. #### Lovelace 1843: Computer Science and Machine Intelligence The first published description of the Analytical Engine was in French, by L. F. Menabrea, 1842[^1]. The English translator, Ada Augusta, Countess of Lovelace, made extensive notes on the science of computer programming, and published her translation in 1843. The notes include her famous program for iteratively computing Bernoulli numbers — arguably the world's first complete computer program — which used conditional jumps to implement the required nested loops. In Lady Lovelace's notes we also find her prescient recognition of the Analytical Engine's power — "In enabling mechanism to combine together general symbols in successions of unlimited variety and extent, a uniting link is established between the operations of matter and the abstract mental processes of the most abstract branch of mathematical science."[^1] Here also we find what Alan Turing later called "Lady Lovelace's Objection"[^2] to the possibility of machine intelligence — "It can do whatever we know how to order it to perform. It can follow analysis; but it has no power of anticipating any analytical relations or truths. Its province is to assist us in making available what we are already acquainted with."[^1] #### Turing 1946: Calls and Returns In 1936 Alan Turing defined his foundational model of computation[^3], designated by Alonzo Church as the Turing Machine[^4]. In 1945 Turing began designing his physical Automatic Computing Engine[^5] (ACE), completing the proposal in early 1946, in which he introduced the concept of calls and returns: _"To start on a subsidiary operation we need only make a note of where we left off the major operation and then apply the first instruction of the subsidiary. When the subsidiary is over we look up the note and continue with the major operation."_ The ACE design was vacuum-tube logic with a memory remarkable for its day: some 25 kilobytes, held in mercury delay lines of 1024 bits — 32 words of 32 bits each — circulating at 1 MHz. The return stack was kept in those delay lines, 32 return addresses to the line. The smaller Pilot ACE was for a time the world's fastest computer. #### Industry Practice: 1945 to present Call and return facilities have proven their worth across eighty years of important machines — under various names (subroutines, procedures, functions, methods) and at various levels of complexity (link registers, return stacks, stack frames). The machines I have programmed or implemented cover much of that line. Their designs differ chiefly in where the return address lives and whether the control flow is static. ##### Physical Machines Cray's CDC series used the self-modifying code of the EDSAC's Wheeler jump; the Cray-1 abandoned it for a link register, like the IBM 360 before it and the ARM and RISC-V since. The PDP-11, VAX, 68000, and x86 push return addresses onto the same stack as data — the stack-frame design that C made universal, and that stack-smashing exploits have abused ever since, precisely because return addresses live where data can overwrite them. None of these facilities are static — they were built for performance all the way down to the silicon, and happily sacrificed static control flow to get it. An outlier, the Burroughs B5000 had protected stack frames and static control flow in 1961, before almost every machine above; it was built for Algol 60, the language famously ahead of nearly all its successors. Except in performance. ##### Virtual Machines Forth, like Turing's ACE, keeps a separate return stack, sealed off from data — the design adopted by the EVM proposals discussed below. The Java Virtual Machine (JVM) in effect does the same, as do .NET's Common Language Runtime (CLR) and WebAssembly (Wasm): bytecode can never touch a return address. These are the EVM's nearest kin — stack machines running portable bytecode from untrusted sources — and so, unlike Forth, which trusts its programmer, they require validated static control flow. The JVM, CLR, Wasm, and others share three crucial properties: * portable bytecode that can be directly interpreted * static control flow that is validated before runtime * compilation to machine code at runtime, in _linear time_ The static control flow that supports linear-time compilers equally supports any other tool that must traverse the control flow of a program: each edge need be traversed only once.
